attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his own post. He is not quoting anyone.

semantics.note: An unhedged present-tense statement about contemporary LLMs. The employee-training comparison is context and is fairly left out.

contract.note: The plain reading (frequent missed clear instructions, not failure on most simple requests) is ordinary and fair. The 2023 window to the post date is a reasonable inference from 'even now'. Retrospective use of later papers is limited to models tested in that window.

evidence.note: IFEval tested PaLM 2 S in August 2023: it fully complied on only about 43% of prompts (strict). This is published retrospective evidence about a model tested in the window. It is a smaller model, and the November GPT-4 results are rightly excluded.

GPT-4 from June 2023 failed nearly all answer-extraction formatting requests and degraded on composite instructions. It followed single formatting instructions well, so its reliability was uneven, not absent.
CELLO (September 2023) shows strengths that vary by task and benchmark, on Chinese complex instructions with partial-credit scoring. Not a representative failure rate.

reviews.rationale: Reproducible evaluations of models from 2023 show frequent, material failures across multiple instruction types: PaLM 2 S fully complied on fewer than half of IFEval prompts, and GPT-4 (June) failed extraction formatting and composite instructions. GPT-4's good results on single instructions show unevenness but do not meet the contradiction condition of consistently reliable compliance. On the contract's plain reading, the claim holds.

attribution.note: Marcus's own assertion in his post.

semantics.note: Accurately restates an unhedged present-tense observation. Reading it as being about LLMs fits the context.

contract.note: Taking 'huge' as needing safeguards in consequential uses, and 'unsolved' as not eliminated (progress allowed), is an ordinary, fair reading.

evidence.note: OpenAI's own GPT-4 disclosure (March 2023) says the model still hallucinates and urges great care and human review in high-stakes uses. It is a company disclosure, but it admits a limitation, and the contract's support condition explicitly accepts model disclosures. It also reports improvement, which does not amount to elimination.

reviews.rationale: In the window, the leading developer itself acknowledged that hallucinations continued and called for safeguards or avoiding high-stakes uses. That meets the support condition. The reported improvements do not show hallucinations were eliminated or made negligible, so the contradiction condition is not met.

attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his post.

semantics.note: Two asserted parts: GPT can't be trusted to follow chess rules, and the rules appear in its training data. 'Probably' qualifies only 'multiple times', so the presence of the rules is asserted.

contract.note: 'Can't be trusted' read as producing illegal moves that need checking is fair and ordinary. Treating the training-data claim as a separate component is fair because he asserted it, but it is hard to verify.

evidence.note: Over 1,000 games, gpt-3.5-turbo-0301 made an illegal move about every four moves. This supports the rule-following part for that one model; GPT-4 and instruct models were not tested.
The GPT-4 report withholds details of how its dataset was built. It neither confirms nor refutes that explicit chess rules were in the training data.

reviews.rationale: The rule-following part is supported for one GPT-3.5 snapshot, which made frequent illegal moves. The contract's support condition also requires credible training documentation that the rules were in the training data, and the packet has none: OpenAI withholds dataset details. Nothing contradicts either part. The other GPT models in use were untested. So the claim as a whole is not settled.

attribution.note: Marcus's own description of the situation in his post.

semantics.note: The revision keeps 'at least partly', the named firms, and reliability as a separate problem. This is faithful.

contract.note: Reading 'bans' as limits on employees' use of external LLM services, not as blanket prohibitions, is the ordinary reading and fair.

evidence.note: May 2023 report on internal documents obtained by the WSJ: Apple restricted employees' use of ChatGPT over fears of leaking confidential information. It also lists other firms with restrictions. This is secondary reporting.
Reports JPMorgan's February restriction (sensitive-data concern, per the Telegraph) plus restrictions at Verizon, Deutsche Bank, Amazon and others, with Verizon's stated confidentiality rationale.
May 2023 primary research shows ChatGPT and GPT-4 giving incorrect answers backed by further false claims. This supports the reliability part.

reviews.rationale: Reporting from within the window documents restrictions at Apple, JPMorgan and several other large employers, with confidentiality concerns as a contributing reason. Primary research documents substantive reliability problems. The full policy histories through September were unavailable, but nothing shows the restrictions were lifted. The support condition is met.
